questions.q: Walk me through how you would build a schedule for a new project from scratch.
questions.test: Whether you plan top-down from constraints before going bottom-up, and whether you involve the people doing the work.
strong: Start from the constraints: date, budget, team and scope
Define milestones with exit criteria before listing tasks
Have leads estimate their own work, and compare with past actuals
Map dependencies and the critical path
Hold explicit buffer before key gates
Set a cadence for re-planning
weak: Jumping straight into a Gantt chart
No buffer, or buffer hidden inside every task
Treating the first plan as fixed
questions.follow: What would you do if the leads' estimates add up to twice the time available?

questions.q: An engineer tells you a task will take two weeks. How do you decide whether to trust that estimate?
questions.test: Calibration and respect: can you probe an estimate without bullying it down?
strong: Ask what is known and unknown, and what it depends on
Ask what else they are working on in that window
Compare with their past estimates against actuals
Use a range, or optimistic, likely and pessimistic
Agree an early check-in point
weak: Accepting it without a single question
questions.follow: How would you handle it if the estimate turned out to be badly wrong?

questions.q: How do you handle a milestone that is going to slip?
questions.test: Early detection, real options, and honest communication.
strong: Spot it early through tracking, not at the deadline
Quantify how far and why
Lay out options: cut scope, move the date, add resources, with trade-offs
Get the decision from the right person
Communicate early, before anyone is surprised
questions.follow: Which of those options do you reach for first, and why?

questions.q: What is the difference between a roadmap and a schedule?
questions.test: Whether you plan at the right altitude for the right audience.
strong: A roadmap is what and why, at milestone level, and changes deliberately
A schedule is who does what and when, at task level, and changes constantly
You need both, connected
weak: Treating them as the same document
questions.follow: Who is the audience for each?

questions.q: How much buffer do you build into a plan, and where do you put it?
questions.test: Whether buffer is an honest, managed tool or a hidden cushion.
strong: Explicit, visible buffer before major gates
Sized to risk: more for new tech, new teams and certification
Tracked separately, with what consumed it logged
Never spent on new features
weak: A single buffer month at the very end
questions.follow: What do you say when leadership asks you to remove it?

questions.q: A director wants to add a major feature two months before content lock. What do you do?
questions.test: Making trade-offs visible instead of reflexively saying yes or no.
strong: Understand why they want it and what problem it solves
Estimate the cost with the leads
Show what moves or gets cut to make room
Present options and let the right person decide
Document the decision and its impact
weak: Adding it with no impact assessment
questions.follow: What if the director insists on both the feature and the date?

questions.q: How do you decide what to cut when you are out of time?
questions.test: A clear framework that protects the core experience.
strong: Protect the core loop and what makes the game itself
Rank by player impact against cost and risk
Prefer cutting whole features over degrading everything
Involve leads, and communicate the why
weak: Cutting whatever is least far along
questions.follow: Give me an example of something you cut and how the team took it.

questions.q: How do you prevent scope creep without killing creativity?
questions.test: Whether you can channel ideas rather than block them.
strong: A change process: new work in, existing work out, with the cost visible
A parking lot for ideas so nothing is lost
Exploration in pre-production, a feature freeze at alpha
Make the cost of every change visible
questions.follow: Who owns the decision when a new idea arrives mid-production?

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to reduce scope. How did you get the team on board?
questions.test: Real experience of a hard trade-off, and how you handled the people side.
strong: A specific situation, the constraint, and the decision
How you involved the team rather than imposing it
What you protected and why
The outcome, and what you would repeat
weak: Taking all the credit, or none of the responsibility
questions.follow: What did you learn about how to deliver that news?

questions.q: What are the biggest risks on a typical game project, and how do you track them?
questions.test: Structured risk thinking rather than vague worry.
strong: Categories: schedule, technical, team, external or platform, market
A risk register with probability, impact, owner, mitigation and contingency
A regular review cadence
Escalation for the highest-scoring risks
weak: A register created at kickoff and never reviewed
questions.follow: What is the risk you see most teams underestimate?

questions.q: What is the difference between mitigation and contingency?
questions.test: A basic but revealing piece of risk vocabulary.
strong: Mitigation acts before the risk lands, to reduce its probability or impact
Contingency is the plan for after it lands
You usually want both
weak: Treating them as the same thing
questions.follow: Give an example of each for losing a key team member.

questions.q: Your only engineer who understands the netcode has just resigned. What do you do in the first week?
questions.test: Calm prioritization under pressure, technical and human.
strong: Use the notice period for knowledge transfer: documentation, pairing, recorded walkthroughs
Re-plan the milestones that depend on that system
Line up contractor or internal options
Tell stakeholders early with a plan
Check on how the rest of the team is doing
weak: Panic, or no plan for knowledge transfer
questions.follow: How would you stop this being a single point of failure next time?

questions.q: How do you write a status report for executives?
questions.test: Clear, honest written communication for a busy audience.
strong: Short, with the headline and any bad news first
Clear status definitions, not decoration
Decisions needed, stated explicitly
Trends over time, not just a snapshot
The same format every time
weak: Everything green until suddenly it is red
questions.follow: What does your red, amber or green actually mean?

questions.q: How do you keep a publisher informed without creating panic?
questions.test: Managing an external relationship with transparency and control.
strong: A regular cadence, so updates are routine
No surprises: raise risks early, with mitigation
Milestone definitions agreed in advance
Data and builds, not just reassurance
questions.follow: Tell me how you would raise a likely milestone miss with them.

questions.q: How do you explain a technical risk to a non-technical stakeholder?
questions.test: Translation without distortion.
strong: Translate it into impact on date, cost, quality or players
Present options and what each costs
Avoid jargon
Have the engineer check your summary
weak: Passing on the technical detail unfiltered
Minimizing the risk to avoid a hard conversation
questions.follow: What if the stakeholder asks you to commit to a date anyway?

questions.q: How would you tell the team the game is being delayed?
questions.test: Honesty and care in a hard internal message.
strong: Tell them early, before the public
Give the real reasons
Say what changes and what does not
Explain how you will protect their time
Leave room for questions
weak: Letting them find out from social media or the press
A PR version for the team
questions.follow: What would you do in the weeks after the announcement?

questions.q: Two leads disagree on a creative direction and work is stalling. What do you do?
questions.test: Facilitating a decision rather than splitting the difference.
strong: Hear both perspectives properly
Reframe around the game's goals and pillars
Make it clear who decides, and by when
Document the decision and the reasoning
Follow up with both people afterwards
weak: Averaging the two visions by default
Taking a side to end the argument
questions.follow: What if the decision-maker is one of the two people arguing?

questions.q: How do you handle a team member who keeps missing commitments?
questions.test: Fairness, curiosity and directness.
strong: A private conversation first
Find the cause: blockers, overload, unclear expectations or something personal
Clarify what is expected and agree next steps
Escalate to their manager if it continues
weak: Calling it out in a group meeting
questions.follow: What if the cause turns out to be the schedule you set?

questions.q: How do you protect a team from burnout during a hard push?
questions.test: Whether you see crunch as a planning failure to be managed, not a culture.
strong: Limit the duration and define the end
Prioritize ruthlessly so the push is on what matters
Watch for warning signs and act on them
Model sustainable behavior yourself
Plan recovery time afterwards
questions.follow: How do you prevent the next one?

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to deliver difficult news to a director or executive.
questions.test: Courage and judgment in upward communication.
strong: A specific situation and why it was hard
How you prepared: data, options, a recommendation
How you delivered it, and the result
What you would do the same or differently
weak: A version where you were simply right and they were wrong
questions.follow: How did it affect the relationship afterwards?

questions.q: How do you adapt Scrum for game development?
questions.test: Practical judgment rather than textbook answers.
strong: Sprints suit production work with clear deliverables
Pre-production exploration fits time-boxed experiments or kanban better
Milestones sit above sprints
A definition of done that works for art, design and code
questions.follow: Where have you seen Scrum fail on a game?

questions.q: When would you use Kanban instead of Scrum?
questions.test: Matching the process to the shape of the work.
strong: Flow work: live ops, bug fixing, art pipelines, support
Work with highly variable cycle times
Small teams that need less ceremony
weak: No real distinction between the two
questions.follow: How would you measure whether it is working?

questions.q: How do you run a retrospective that actually changes something?
questions.test: Whether retros produce change rather than venting.
strong: Psychological safety so people speak honestly
Start by reviewing the last retro's actions
Leave with one or two owned, specific actions
Follow through, and escalate repeat issues
weak: Long lists of actions nobody owns
questions.follow: What do you do when the same problem comes up three retros in a row?

questions.q: What tools have you used, and how would you choose one for a team?
questions.test: Tool fluency, and choosing for the team rather than for yourself.
strong: Names real tools you have used and for what
Chooses by team size, workflow and integration needs
One source of truth
Adoption matters more than features
weak: Never having used any tracker seriously
questions.follow: How would you move a team from one tool to another?

questions.q: How would you plan the first six months after launch of a live game?
questions.test: Whether you understand that live games are operated, not finished.
strong: A season or update cadence players can rely on
Content staggered: one beat live, the next in production, the one after in pre-production
Live ops readiness: on-call rota, rollback plan, incident communications
Metrics that tell you what to build next
Season two in production before launch
weak: A content calendar with no connection to retention
questions.follow: What would you cut first if the team were half the size?

questions.q: What metrics would you watch in the first 30 days of a live game?
questions.test: Knowing the numbers that matter and what you would do with them.
strong: Retention by cohort (day one, day seven, day thirty)
Stability: crash rate, server health, error rates
Concurrency and session patterns
Funnel drop-off points in onboarding and progression
Monetization metrics if free-to-play
Player sentiment
weak: Metrics with no plan for acting on them
questions.follow: Retention is lower than forecast at day seven. What do you do?

questions.q: A critical bug goes live on a Friday evening. Walk me through what happens.
questions.test: Incident management and keeping a cool head.
strong: Confirm severity and impact quickly
Bring in the on-call people who can act
Decide between hotfix, rollback or a server-side change
Communicate to players and internally, on a schedule
Run a blameless postmortem afterwards
weak: The producer as a bottleneck for every decision
questions.follow: How do you decide whether to roll back?

questions.q: How do you balance live operations with building the next big update?
questions.test: Protecting roadmap capacity from constant interruption.
strong: Separate capacity for live ops, such as a rotation, from feature work
An explicit interrupt budget
Clear severity rules for what can interrupt the roadmap
weak: Everyone does everything, all the time
questions.follow: How would you handle a quarter where live issues ate the whole budget?

questions.q: What happens between alpha and launch?
questions.test: A working knowledge of milestones and release work.
strong: Alpha as feature complete, beta as content complete
Code lock and the release candidate
Certification on console, with resubmission time
Localization, ratings, store assets and marketing beats
A day-one patch plan
questions.follow: Where does buffer belong in that stretch?

questions.q: How do you plan for console certification?
questions.test: Respect for a gate you can fail.
strong: Read the platform requirements early and design for them
A named compliance owner
An internal pre-certification pass
Time for at least one resubmission
Age ratings secured in advance
Plan certification for the day-one patch too
weak: Treating certification as a formality at the end
questions.follow: What tends to fail certification for first-time teams?

questions.q: What would be on your launch-week checklist?
questions.test: Operational readiness, not just shipping the build.
strong: Final builds approved on every platform
Store pages, pricing and release timing checked
Review keys and creator outreach done
Crash reporting and monitoring live
Community and support ready
On-call and hotfix plan in place
weak: No plan for the first 48 hours
questions.follow: What do you watch in the first hour after release?

questions.q: How do you know whether a project is healthy?
questions.test: Leading indicators, not just a green status.
strong: Progress against milestone exit criteria
Velocity trend against plan
How fast buffer is being used
The bug curve
The risk register's trend
Team morale and attrition signals
weak: Relying on people saying it is fine
questions.follow: Which indicator moves first when a project is about to go wrong?

questions.q: How do you use velocity, and what are its limits?
questions.test: Using a metric without abusing it.
strong: For forecasting within one stable team
Not comparable across teams
Not a performance score for individuals
Only meaningful with consistent estimation
weak: Using it to compare teams or rank people
questions.follow: What would you do if velocity suddenly dropped?

questions.q: How do you develop junior producers?
questions.test: Whether you build people, not just schedules.
strong: Give them ownership of a real workstream
Coach with regular, specific feedback
Let them stretch where failure is recoverable
Have honest career conversations
questions.follow: How do you know when someone is ready for more scope?

questions.q: How would you structure production for a 100-person team?
questions.test: Scaling production without drowning in process.
strong: Feature or pod teams with embedded producers
A central function for cross-team dependencies and milestones
Consistent tools and reporting
Clear decision rights at each level
questions.follow: Where do cross-team dependencies get resolved?

questions.q: How do you build trust with a creative director?
questions.test: Partnership rather than gatekeeping.
strong: Understand and champion their vision
Make their goals the plan's goals
No surprises, ever
Data-informed trade-offs, presented as options
Clear agreement on who decides what
questions.follow: What do you do when you think their direction puts the date at risk?

questions.q: Describe how you would take over a project that is already in trouble.
questions.test: Diagnosis before prescription.
strong: Listen first, through one-on-ones
Assess the real state: build, backlog, risks, morale
A few early wins to rebuild confidence
Re-baseline the plan with honest dates
Communicate the new plan clearly, and change process gradually
weak: Arriving with a new process on day one
questions.follow: What would you change in your first 30 days?

questions.q: Tell me about the biggest mistake you have made as a producer.
questions.test: Self-awareness and genuine learning.
strong: A real mistake with real consequences
Clear ownership
What you changed afterwards, and evidence it worked
questions.follow: How would you spot the same mistake earlier now?

questions.q: Tell me about a project that shipped late. What would you do differently?
questions.test: Honest postmortem thinking.
strong: The specific causes, not just 'scope creep'
When the signals appeared and how you responded
Concrete changes you would make
weak: Blaming the team, or taking all the blame
questions.follow: What was the earliest signal you missed?

questions.q: Tell me about a time you influenced a decision without having authority.
questions.test: Influence, which is most of a producer's real power.
strong: The situation and who held the decision
How you built the case: data, allies, options
The outcome and what you learned
weak: A story with no clear outcome
questions.follow: What would you have done if they had said no?
